headline:Iran may be restoring activity at nuclear-linked site struck by Israel

The Institute for Science and International Security (ISIS) said Saturday that satellite imagery showed repairs to what appeared to be a water tank and the addition of a small building nearby at the Minzadayi compound, northeast of Tehran.

The findings add to an assessment published Tuesday in which the institute identified unusually heavy vehicle traffic and earth-moving activity at the heavily secured site, which Israeli aircraft struck on March 3.

The latest observations suggest Iran is seeking “not just to clean up the site” but to resume regular activities there, the institute said in a post on X.

Iran has consistently denied seeking nuclear weapons, maintaining that its nuclear program is intended for peaceful purposes.

The International Atomic Energy Agency has said it has no credible indication of a coordinated Iranian nuclear weapons program, although it has repeatedly raised concerns about Tehran's uranium enrichment and unresolved questions over past nuclear activities.

The original ISIS report, based on high-resolution satellite images taken in September and October, documented passenger vehicles and trucks returning to the compound following extensive work to remove rubble and repair damage from the Israeli attack.

Researchers also identified continued excavation at a section of the compound where the March strikes had left several craters, apparently above underground structures.

The institute said the activity could indicate an attempt to restore capabilities associated with nuclear weapons development. But the images do not establish what work, if any, has resumed inside the compound.

Israel identified Minzadayi as a covert nuclear weapons development facility during the war, saying scientists there had been working on a component of a nuclear weapons system. The institute's assessment of the site's earlier purpose relies partly on those Israeli military claims, which have not been independently verified.

The US and Israel launched their military campaign against Iran on February 28, two days after indirect nuclear negotiations in Geneva that Omani mediators said had made progress. Further technical talks had been planned before the attacks began.

Washington and Tehran remain divided over the future of Iran's nuclear program. The Trump administration is demanding substantial reductions in Iran's enrichment capacity, while Tehran insists it will not surrender its right to enrich uranium.

On Saturday, the Kremlin said Russian President Vladimir Putin had conveyed Tehran's position on a possible settlement of the war to President Donald Trump during a phone call Friday, following consultations with Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian.

Moscow disclosed neither the details of Iran's position nor Trump's response.

The institute's findings raise the possibility that Iran is rebuilding infrastructure damaged in the war, but leave unanswered the more consequential question of whether any nuclear weapons-related research has resumed.
